stem: Several similar healthcare-associated infections are identified on one unit. Which response best reflects a systematic outbreak investigation?

options.A: Verify the diagnoses and outbreak, alert key partners, define and find cases, analyze data by person/place/time, develop and test hypotheses, and implement control measures as evidence becomes available.
options.B: Select the most likely source immediately and design all control actions around that assumption without systematic case finding or data analysis.
options.C: Wait until the cluster becomes large before beginning an investigation because smaller clusters do not warrant epidemiologic assessment.
options.D: Keep the investigation within the public-health team and avoid collaboration with facility clinicians, laboratory personnel, and infection-prevention staff.

rationale: A is correct. CDC describes outbreak and healthcare-associated infection investigations as systematic, multistep processes that include verifying the diagnosis and outbreak, communicating with key partners, establishing case definitions, identifying and counting cases, organizing data by person, place, and time, formulating and testing hypotheses, implementing control measures, and communicating findings. Steps may occur concurrently, and preliminary control measures may be appropriate before the entire investigation is complete. B anchors prematurely without evidence. C is incorrect because even a single unusual healthcare-associated case can trigger a full investigation depending on the disease and setting. D conflicts with CDC's emphasis on collaboration among public-health officials, facility staff, clinicians, laboratories, and other stakeholders.
educational_objective: Participate in outbreak response as a systematic, collaborative process of case verification and finding, descriptive and analytic epidemiology, hypothesis testing, and timely implementation of evidence-informed control measures.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual — Conducting a Field Investigation; Healthcare Settings
source_version_date: Conducting a Field Investigation dated January 6, 2025; Healthcare Settings current CDC page accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Conducting a Field Investigation — Investigation/Ten Steps: systematic multistep approach; diagnosis/outbreak confirmation may occur together; early collaboration is important; Step 6 notes control measures can be implemented at any point and modified as evidence evolves. Healthcare Settings — Field Investigation: verify diagnosis, confirm HAI outbreak, alert key partners, establish case definitions, identify/count cases, organize person/place/time data, formulate/test hypotheses, perform infection-control assessment/control measures, follow up and communicate findings.
source_claim_supported: Healthcare outbreak investigations use a systematic, collaborative sequence of diagnosis/outbreak verification, case definition and finding, descriptive analysis, hypothesis development/testing, control measures, and communication; steps may overlap and smaller signals can still warrant investigation.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: collaborate with multidisciplinary teams, participate in quality-improvement and safety activities, and coordinate responses to changes affecting groups of clients.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — collaborative healthcare outbreak investigation
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw summary item with CDC's current healthcare-setting investigation sequence and corrected two overstatements: investigations are not limited by outbreak size, and control measures need not always wait until every analytic step is complete.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current CDC Field Epidemiology Manual chapters, including the healthcare-specific investigation sequence.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A contains the CDC sequence and allows overlapping actions. B commits premature causal attribution. C falsely requires a large outbreak. D rejects required collaboration.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; systematic and collaborative outbreak response.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; hypotheses should be generated and tested using case/data analysis.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; investigation threshold depends on the event and setting, not only cluster size.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A preserves both systematic epidemiology and the flexibility for concurrent control measures.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices describe plausible outbreak-response strategies.
audit_findings.blueprint: Facility/public-health coordination and safety response fit Management of Care.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked step order and avoided implying a rigid linear sequence. The final item explicitly accommodates concurrent steps and early controls when warranted. No second answer remained.
